title: Project: line filter
goal: Filter complete lines by prefix and count each rejected record separately.

prerequisites.text: Be able to handle input statuses and compare a whole string and its beginning.

terms.title: Prefix
terms.definition: The bytes starting at position 0. Prefix matching checks the start of a string.

terms.title: Rejected record
terms.definition: A record that exceeds the length limit or contains a null byte.

terms.title: Filter
terms.definition: A rule that selects or skips a whole record.

sections.title: Several entries from a log
paragraphs: A log receives messages. The reader checks whether each record is usable based on its length and termination. Then the filter compares the start of each valid line. Test those decisions with separate inputs.
CORRUPT can be a valid line that the filter skips. An overlong line increments rejected regardless of its text.
Consume the rest of a rejected line through its boundary. The next read_line call then starts on the first byte of the next message.
Counting damaged records and selecting valid ones solve different problems. Valid text without the prefix does not increase rejected.

Classify a three-record log. A short INFO record lacks the needed beginning but is usable text. A long record with the right tag cannot be accepted as a whole string. A short accepted record with the right tag reaches output. Decide which outcome a record has before deciding whether to update the counter.

sections.title: Select the lines starting with ID:
paragraphs: First work through prefix selection on three known strings. The program compares the first three bytes of each one, then prints each whole matching line.

The ID: example starts with an array of valid strings. This deliberately removes the reader so you can observe selection alone. In the project, put the reader first and keep prefix comparison on the accepted-record branch.
steps: ID:7 begins with matching I, D and colon bytes. The output includes ID:7.
XID:7 begins with X. The program skips it.
ID: ends after the matching prefix. The program prints it too.

sections.title: Use a separate input for each rule
paragraphs: ERR fan exposes an exact-line comparison when the task requires a prefix. XERR shows why prefix matching starts at position 0.
A long record followed by a short line checks both the buffer limit and where reading resumes. A null byte rejects the whole record before comparison.
The third argument to strncmp specifies a byte count. The separate diagnostic passes the string "3". Clang reports that this argument needs an integer.

sections.title: Design a filter for a different log
paragraphs: Imagine a log with prefix WARN and an eight-byte limit. Pick a normal match, a record with WARN in the middle and an overlong record. Write down the complete expected stdout and the count.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Check how getchar reports the end of input and how strcmp and strncmp differ.

selfcheck.prompt: Why is XID:7 absent from the example output?
options: ID: must be the whole line
feedback: The example uses known strings in an array.
ID:7 includes more text after the prefix and still matches.

selfcheck.prompt: What happens to a blank record in the project?
options: The reader accepts it and the filter skips it
feedback: The blank line fits and has a terminator in the buffer.
It lacks prefix ERR, so the filter skips it.
Reading continues after a blank line.

selfcheck.prompt: How can you test that a rejected record was drained, and why does an overlong record containing NUL increment rejected once?
selfcheck.feedback: Supply an overlong record followed by ERR ok. The second line should be preserved and the count should rise by 1. The reader returns one result for a whole record, so the two reasons still count as one rejection.

practice.title: Project: filter the log
practice.task: Read records until EOF. A record can hold at most 12 text bytes. Print each valid record whose first bytes are exactly ERR, preserving its text. LF and CRLF delimit records. Handle a final record with data before EOF. An overlong record or a record containing a null byte increments rejected once after it is consumed. Skip valid lines without the prefix. Finish with rejected, a space and the rejected count. Fix the selection condition and keep the supplied input reader and counter.
practice.stdin:
OK
ERR fan
ERR
 ERR
ERR verylongdata
practice.hint: Check the result of reading a record first. Then ask whether the first three bytes match.
criteria: ERR fan and ERR are printed in full. A leading space before ERR prevents a match.
Twelve bytes fit. Thirteen cause a rejection and preserve the start of the next line.
A record containing a null byte increases rejected even if it starts with ERR.
The final line rejected N follows all matches.
Cases marked “automatic WASI check” use exact bytes. Read their labels and expected output. You can enter the other cases in the lesson editor.

steps.action: Run the starter with the supplied log.
steps.why: It contains an exact match, an overlong line and a matching prefix with more text.
steps.expected: The starter prints only ERR and rejected 1.

steps.action: Fix the comparison of the opening bytes and rerun.
steps.why: A valid record qualifies when its first three bytes match ERR.
steps.expected: The output now includes ERR fan, ERR and rejected 1.

steps.action: Follow an overlong line with ERR done. In a separate run, enter ERR fan without a final LF.
steps.why: Check the next record and data that reaches EOF.
steps.expected: The first run preserves ERR done and gives rejected 1. The second gives ERR fan and rejected 0.

exercises.title: Try it on your own
exercises.task: In the lesson editor, after saving a copy of main.c in a separate text file, use prefix WARN, a comparison count of 4 and a limit of 8. Supply WARN ok, XWARN and WARN too long. Add another valid match after the overlong line. Check the labelled WASI cases against their expected output. Restore your saved main.c after the experiment.
criteria: The first three records produce only WARN ok, then rejected 1.
The extra match is printed in full before the total.

teaching.scene: Log tags appear at the start of records. Build a rule that retains the matching text in full and keeps a checkable count of damaged records.

predict.prompt: The listing receives ID:7, XID:7 and ID:. Which records does it print, and why does the record with the tag inside behave differently?
predict.answer: It prints ID:7 and ID:. Their first three bytes equal ID:. XID:7 starts with X, so its prefix check fails.

apply.prompt: For a 12-byte limit and the ERR prefix, feed ERR long example, XERR and ERR z in that order. The last record has no newline. Predict both parts of the report and explain how the decisions for the first two records differ.
apply.answer: The program prints ERR z and rejected 1 on separate lines. The first record is too long and increments the counter. XERR is valid but starts with X and is simply skipped. The last record contains data, so it is processed at EOF.

practice.strategy: Start with a short accepted match and a record that does not match. Once selection works, put an overlong record before a match. Predict stdout and rejected separately so you can identify the stage where the result diverges.
practice.diagnosis: If the count is right but ERR fan is missing, the reader might already be correct. How many bytes should your comparison cover, and what text should reach output?

syntax.explanation: strncmp from <string.h> limits the comparison to the given number of bytes. Prefix ID: requires all three bytes, including the colon.
syntax.mistake: A whole-string comparison rejects a record with the right beginning and extra text. Compare the number of bytes in the prefix.
